summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory. Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate across the parts of it under Moroccan control, and a visitor there stands under Moroccan law wherever those institutions act. Human Rights Watch recorded that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. A PinkNews global legality roundup of July 2017 lists the SADR as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, states that it has been illegal there for decades, and records the status as criminalised for July 2017.

Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA all describe same-sex sexual activity as illegal in the SADR for both males and females, punishable by up to three years in prison. Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims.

The claimant state's own institutions are recorded enforcing that prohibition. A 2009 report from USCRI found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape.

The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'; CEAR concludes that this silence leaves no legal protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence.
tangentialFactors:
The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalised in Spain until 1979. That sequence shapes the legal and social inheritance a visitor encounters, since the criminal provisions in force outlasted the decriminalisation that took effect in the former administering country.

Most residents of the territory are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon, which raises the social cost of visible non-conformity independently of what any statute says. The absence of a protection mechanism compounds this: CEAR records no avenue against discrimination or violence for LGBTQ people in the claimant state's jurisdiction.

Two legal layers run in parallel. Where Moroccan institutions operate, the Moroccan penal code and its police discretion govern; the SADR layer, asserted over the territory and exercised concretely in the Algeria-based refugee camps, records its own detention of people on homosexuality charges. Neither layer is documented as offering gender-identity protection.

The 2005 prosecution of seven human-rights defenders shows the wider environment of control around assembly and speech in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, the same terrain on which morality provisions are applied.
localsOnly:
Sahrawi residents in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara face the Moroccan penal code in Moroccan courts, as the seven human-rights defenders tried on protest-fomenting charges in 2005 demonstrate; Human Rights Watch judged those charges dubious.

Residents of the Algeria-based refugee camps administered by the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic are subject to that government's authorities. A 2009 USCRI report recorded officials there holding prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while describing conduct that would more fittingly be rape.

No statutory protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence exists in the claimant state's framework. CEAR documents this absence, and the 2010 statement by Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, that the Constitution neither refers to homosexuality nor punishes it leaves the prohibition resting on other provisions rather than an express constitutional text.

Socially, most residents are Muslim and same-sex relationships are regarded as a foreign phenomenon, so openly trans or gender-nonconforming residents have no domestic constituency to appeal to when they are targeted.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses trans identity directly. Gender markers on identity documents, entry or border screening that could out a visitor, bathroom and facility access, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, and access to gender-affirming care in Western Sahara are all unsourced for this territory and should be treated as unresolved rather than assumed either way.

Whether the six-month-to-three-year penalty attached to same-sex conduct has in practice been applied to a trans person in the territory is not sourced. The claim that police morality discretion is the instrument turned on visibly trans people rests on the general structure of the Moroccan provisions as described here, not on a documented case in Western Sahara.

The divergence between the Moroccan penal framework and whatever the SADR would apply as state law is unresolved: the sources give a penalty figure for the SADR (up to three years) and a separate range for the Moroccan framework, but do not establish how gender-identity offences, as distinct from same-sex conduct, are treated under either.

The most recent territory-specific status entry is dated July 2017, and no source records enforcement, prosecution or protection developments after that date.
